nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham theorem on Poincare--Einstein metrics
nodes.statement: It was shown that a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric is determined by specifying a conformal metric on its boundary, together with an ``obstruction tensor'', and solving Einstein's equations order by order in powers of the ``radial'' coordinate.
nodes.statement_short: A Poincare--Einstein metric is determined by its boundary conformal metric and an obstruction tensor, solving Einstein's equations order by order.
conclusions: is determined by specifying a conformal metric on its boundary, together with an ``obstruction tensor'', and solving Einstein's equations order by order in powers of the ``radial'' coordinate

nodes.name: Conformally compact Riemannian manifold
nodes.statement_short: $(M,g)$ is conformally compact if a boundary defining function $\rho$ makes $\rho^2 g$ extend to the boundary, restricting to a metric $\gamma_{(0)}$.
differentia: $\rho^2 g$ can be extended continuously to $X$

nodes.name: Hyperbolic space as a conformally compact manifold
Hyperbolic metric on the upper half-space
nodes.statement: g=\frac{dx^2+dy^2+dz^2+dt^2}{t^2},

nodes.name: Non-uniqueness of the defining function
nodes.statement: It is important to note that the defining function $\rho$ is non-unique: for any positive function $\lambda$ on $\overline{M}$, we may consider $\tilde\rho=\lambda\rho$ which has the same properties above with $\gamma_{(0)}$ replaced by $\tilde\gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^2\gamma_{(0)}$. Therefore a conformally compact metric on $M$ only defines a conformal structure on the boundary $X=\partial \overline{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling $\rho\to\lambda\rho$ rescales $\gamma_{(0)}$ by $\lambda^2$, so only a boundary conformal structure is defined.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A hyperbolic metric is by definition a metric having a constant sectional curvature $-1/l^2$, where $l$ has units of length.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A conformally compact metric $g$ is called \emph{asymptotically hyperbolic} if its sectional curvature is asymptotically $-1/l^2$.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic space is asymptotically hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Obviously, $\mathbb {H}^4$ being conformally compact and hyperbolic is in particular asymptotically hyperbolic.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic condition via $|d\rho|_g$
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic hyperbolicity is equivalent to $|d\rho|^2_g=\rho^2/l^2$ on the boundary, read off from the leading Riemann tensor.
conclusions: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is equivalent to $|d\rho|^2_{g}=\rho^2/l^2$ at $X$

nodes.name: Poincare--Einstein metric
nodes.statement: We also see from this formula that conformally compact Einstein metrics, i.e.\ ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations, are automatically asymptotically hyperbolic; they are called \emph{Poincar\'e--Einstein metrics}.
nodes.statement_short: Conformally compact Einstein metrics, automatically asymptotically hyperbolic, are called Poincare--Einstein metrics.
differentia: satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations

nodes.name: Cosmological constant in terms of curvature radius
nodes.statement: \Lambda = - \frac{3}{l^2}.

nodes.name: Normal form of a conformally compact metric near the boundary
nodes.statement:
Near the boundary $X$, we can write any conformally compact metric as
\begin{eqnarray} g=\frac{l^2}{ \rho^2}\Big(\alpha d\rho^2+d\rho\otimes\beta+\beta\otimes d\rho+\gamma\Big),
\end{eqnarray}
where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are 1-parameter families of functions, 1-forms and symmetric $(2,0)$-tensors on $X$, with the following power series expansion
\[ \alpha=1+\rho\alpha_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad\beta=\beta_{(0)}+\rho\beta_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots. \]
nodes.statement_short: Near the boundary any conformally compact metric is $l^2\rho^{-2}(\alpha d\rho^2+$ mixed $\beta$ terms $+\gamma)$ with power series coefficients.
conclusions: we can write any conformally compact metric as

nodes.name: Conformally compact metric near the boundary
nodes.statement: g=\frac{l^2}{ \rho^2}\Big(\alpha d\rho^2+d\rho\otimes\beta+\beta\otimes d\rho+\gamma\Big),
nodes.label: cc-metric

nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham normal form of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: AH means $\alpha=1$; a diffeomorphism (gradient flow of $\rho$) removes $\beta$, giving $g=l^2\rho^{-2}(d\rho^2+\gamma)$.
conclusions: we can always achieve $\beta=0$ by an appropriate diffeomorphism
we can thus write the metric in the form:

nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham normal form
nodes.statement: g=\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}d\rho^2+\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\gamma \qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots.
nodes.label: FG

nodes.name: Residual diffeomorphism freedom in the metric setting
nodes.statement: There still remains some diffeomorphism freedom: infinitesimal diffeomorphisms generated by vector fields $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ where the function $\lambda$ is $\rho$-independent and the vector field $\xi$ satisfies a certain condition. We thus have, essentially, a residual boundary diffeomorphism as well as freedom of local rescalings of the radial coordinate. The latter is equivalent to the freedom of conformal rescalings of the boundary metric.
nodes.statement_short: Residual boundary diffeomorphisms and radial rescalings, equivalent to boundary conformal rescalings, preserve the normal form.

nodes.name: Order-by-order solution of Einstein's equations in the Fefferman--Graham gauge
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_{(1)}=0$, $\gamma_{(2)}$ is a Schouten-type tensor, $\gamma_{(3)}$ is free but traceless and divergence-free, and higher terms are determined.
conclusions: The first two terms are given by
the third remains undetermined but constrained to satisfy $$\gamma_{(0)}^{ab}\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0,\qquad \nabla_{(0)}{}^a\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0.$$
The remaining, higher-order terms, are then recursively determined algebraically from the previous terms.

nodes.name: Obstruction (Fefferman--Graham)
nodes.statement: The unconstrained part of $\gamma_{(3)ab}$ is referred to as the {\it obstruction} by Fefferman-Graham.

nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham expansion
nodes.statement: We can interpret the expansion (\ref{FG}) as an instance of the initial value problem. Given the initial data on the boundary in the form of the boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$, as well as the constrained $\gamma_{(3)}$, which is best thought of as an initial momentum, we can propagate these data into the bulk, obtaining a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric, at least formally in a neighbourhood of the boundary. This is known as the \emph{Fefferman--Graham expansion}.
nodes.statement_short: Propagating boundary data $\gamma_{(0)}$ and the constrained $\gamma_{(3)}$ into the bulk as an initial value problem gives a Poincare--Einstein metric.

nodes.name: Expansion of the boundary volume density
nodes.statement:
Using the tracelessness of $\gamma_{(3)}$, an easy calculation gives
\begin{eqnarray}\nonumber
\sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma)} = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1+\frac{1}{2} \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(0)}^{-1} \gamma_{(2)})+ O(\rho^4) \right) = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right),
\end{eqnarray}
where we have used (\ref{gamma-2}) to get the second equality.
nodes.statement_short: $\sqrt{\det\gamma}=\sqrt{\det\gamma_{(0)}}(1-\rho^2R_{(0)}/8+O(\rho^4))$.
conclusions: \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma)} = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1+\frac{1}{2} \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(0)}^{-1} \gamma_{(2)})+ O(\rho^4) \right) = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right),

nodes.name: Cut-off volume $V_\epsilon$
Cut-off volume integral
nodes.statement: V_\epsilon =  l^4 \int_\epsilon \frac{d\rho}{\rho^4} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right),

nodes.name: Renormalised volume (metric setting)
nodes.statement:
Thus, the volume is given by
\begin{eqnarray}\nonumber
V_\epsilon = \frac{l^4 }{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} - \frac{l^4 }{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} + {\rm finite\,\,\, terms},
\end{eqnarray}
and the renormalised volume is then defined as
\begin{eqnarray} RV:=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left(  V_\epsilon -\frac{l^4}{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} + \frac{l^4}{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} \right).
\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $V_\epsilon$ diverges like $\epsilon^{-3}$ and $\epsilon^{-1}$; subtracting these counter terms and letting $\epsilon\to0$ defines the renormalised volume $RV$.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume $RV$
nodes.statement: RV:=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left(  V_\epsilon -\frac{l^4}{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} + \frac{l^4}{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} \right).
nodes.label: RV

nodes.name: Conformal invariance of the renormalised volume
nodes.statement: We note that the renormalized volume is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$.
conclusions: is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$

nodes.name: Proof of conformal invariance of the renormalised volume
nodes.statement: In fact for another representative $\tilde \gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^{2}\gamma_{(0)}$, the corresponding defining function is $\tilde \rho=\lambda\rho$ for an appropriate extension of $\lambda$ from the boundary into the bulk, and $\tilde{\epsilon}=\lambda^2 \epsilon$. Then the formula (\ref{RV}) takes exactly the same form in terms of the tilded quantities, which shows that it does not matter which representative in the conformal class of the boundary is used to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: rescaling $\rho$ and $\epsilon$ leaves formula (7) unchanged in tilded quantities.

nodes.name: SO(3)-connection and curvature 2-forms $F^i$
nodes.statement: Let $A^i$ be an ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection on a 4-manifold $M$, and $F^i = dA^i + (1/2) \epsilon^{ijk} A^j\wedge A^k$ be its curvature 2-forms.

nodes.name: Matrix of auxiliary fields $M^{ij}$
nodes.statement: Let $M^{ij}$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix of auxiliary fields.

nodes.name: Connection action $S[A,M]$
Action $S[A,M]$
nodes.statement: S[A,M] = \int_M {\rm Tr}( M F\wedge F).
nodes.label: action

nodes.name: Constraint hypersurface $g(M)=0$
nodes.statement:
We also impose a constraint on the matrix $M$, that it lie on a co-dimension one hypersurface with defining equation
\begin{eqnarray} g(M)=0
\end{eqnarray}
in the space of symmetric $3\times 3$ matrices, determined by a real valued function $g$.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is constrained to a codimension-one hypersurface $g(M)=0$ in symmetric $3\times3$ matrices.

nodes.name: Einstein hypersurface function $g_{\rm E}$
nodes.statement:
Different hypersurfaces give different field equations; the hypersurface relevant to Einstein connections/metrics is given by
\begin{eqnarray} g_{\rm E}(M) = {\rm Tr}(M^{-1}) - \Lambda,
\end{eqnarray}
where $4\Lambda$ is the scalar curvature.

nodes.name: Einstein hypersurface function
nodes.statement: g_{\rm E}(M) = {\rm Tr}(M^{-1}) - \Lambda,
nodes.label: g-EH

nodes.name: Critical points of the constrained action are Einstein metrics
nodes.statement: The claim is that the critical points of (\ref{action}), with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH}) give rise to Einstein metrics.
assumptions: with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH})
conclusions: the critical points of (\ref{action})
give rise to Einstein metrics

nodes.name: Connection field equation $d_A(MF)=0$
nodes.statement: d_A \left( M^{ij} F^j \right) =0.
nodes.label: eq-A

nodes.name: Auxiliary volume form ${\mathcal V}$
nodes.statement: To do this, we introduce an auxiliary volume form ${\mathcal V}$.

nodes.name: Matrix of curvature wedge products $X^{ij}$
Definition of $X^{ij}$
nodes.statement: F^i\wedge F^j = X^{ij} \,{\mathcal V}.
nodes.label: X

nodes.name: $X$ is defined only up to scale
nodes.statement: Note that a different choice of $\mathcal V$ changes the matrix $X^{ij}$ by multiplication by a function. The matrix $X$ is thus defined intrinsically only up to scale.

nodes.name: Action with Lagrange multiplier $S[A,M,\mu]$
Action with Lagrange multiplier
nodes.statement: S[A,M,\mu] = \int_M \left( {\rm Tr}(M X) - \mu \, g(M) \right) {\mathcal V}.

nodes.name: Euler--Lagrange equation for $M$
nodes.statement: X = \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M}.
nodes.label: eq-M

nodes.name: Matrix derivative $\partial g/\partial M$
nodes.statement:
(Here, we write $\partial g/\partial M$ for the matrix defined by
\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} A^{ji} = dg\Big|_{M}(A)
\]
for all symmetric $A^{ij}$.)

nodes.name: Pure connection formulation
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{eq-M}) can be solved, together with $g(M)=0$, for $M(X)$. This can then be substituted to (\ref{eq-A}) to obtain the ``pure connection'' formulation of field equations, in which we obtain second-order PDE's for the connection. Alternatively, one can insert the solution $M(X)$ back into the Lagrangian to obtain the ``pure connection'' action principle. One can check that the Lagrangian arising this way is just the Legendre transform of the function $g(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Solving for $M(X)$ and substituting gives the pure-connection field equations and action, a Legendre transform of $g$.

nodes.name: First-order strategy for $M$
nodes.statement: However, in many circumstances a more useful approach is not to solve for $M(X)$, but to interpret (\ref{eq-A}) as a first-order PDE on the matrix $M$. Solving it one can then find $X$ from (\ref{eq-M}) and thus obtain a set of first-order PDE's on the connection components. It is this strategy that will be followed below for the asymptotically hyperbolic connections.
nodes.statement_short: Treat the connection equation as a first-order PDE for $M$, then get $X$ and first-order PDEs for the connection.

nodes.name: Derivation of $X$ in terms of $M$ for the Einstein case
nodes.statement: In this case we can rewrite (\ref{eq-M}) as $M X = - \mu M^{-1}$. Taking the trace and using the condition $g_E(M)=0$ we obtain $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic: multiply by $M$, take the trace with $g_E(M)=0$ to solve for $\mu$.

nodes.name: $X$ as a function of $M$ for Einstein connections
nodes.statement:
Thus, all in all for the Einstein case
\begin{eqnarray} X = \frac{1}{\Lambda} {\rm Tr}(M X) M^{-2},
\end{eqnarray}
which gives $X$ in terms of $M$, up to scale.
conclusions: X = \frac{1}{\Lambda} {\rm Tr}(M X) M^{-2},

nodes.name: $X$ in terms of $M$ (Einstein)
nodes.statement: X = \frac{1}{\Lambda} {\rm Tr}(M X) M^{-2},
nodes.label: eq-M-gr

nodes.name: Conformal metric of a connection
nodes.statement_short: The unique conformal structure making the curvature 2-forms $F^i$ self-dual, given by Urbantke-type formula (16); requires $X$ definite.

nodes.name: Urbantke-type formula for the conformal metric
nodes.statement: \sqrt{{\rm det(g)}} \, g_{\mu\nu} \sim \tilde{\epsilon}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \epsilon^{ijk} F^i_{\mu\alpha} F^j_{\nu\beta} F^k_{\gamma\delta}.

nodes.name: Volume form ${\mathcal V}_g$ of the connection metric
Volume form of the connection metric
nodes.statement: - 2\Lambda \, {\mathcal V}_g = {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F).
nodes.label: volume

nodes.name: Action as total volume
nodes.statement: With this choice of volume form, the action (\ref{action}) has the geometric interpretation of the total volume, up to overall scale.  The numerical factor in this formula is adjusted to agree with some conventions introduced later.

nodes.name: Deformed Einstein connections
nodes.statement: An interesting class of deformations of the Einstein condition is obtained by simply changing the codimension-one hypersurface that the matrix $M$ is constrained to lie on, in the action (\ref{action}). This corresponds to changing the function $g$ in the equation $g(M)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Deformed theories are obtained by changing the hypersurface $g(M)=0$ on which $M$ is constrained.

nodes.name: $g_{inst}$ gives self-dual gravity
nodes.statement: Repacing $M$ by $M^{-1}$ in this function, setting $g_{inst}={\rm Tr}(M) - \Lambda$, turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics, see \cite{Herfray:2015fpa} for a discussion of this.
conclusions: turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics

nodes.name: Modified hypersurface function $g_{mod}$
Modified function $g_{mod}$
nodes.statement: g_{mod}(M) = {\rm det}(M) - \Lambda.

nodes.name: Results apply to all deformed theories
nodes.statement: Details of these modified theories will not be important for us here, because we will be solving the arising equations in general for an arbitrary function $g(M)$. All our results below apply equally to the modified theories as well as to GR.

nodes.name: Metric of a deformed Einstein connection
nodes.statement: In the deformed case, one continues to define the metric by the condition that the curvature 2-forms are self-dual. The volume form is then fixed to be a constant multiple of the form ${\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F)$, so that the action (\ref{action}) continues to receive the interpretation of the total volume of the space.

nodes.name: Adapted coframe of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement:
First we choose a local coframe for $g$ adapted to the chosen conformal compactification
$$\theta^i=\frac{l}{\rho}e^i,\qquad\theta^4=\frac{l}{\rho}d\rho,$$
where $e^i$ denotes a 1-parameter family of local coframes for the 1-parameter family of metrics $\gamma$ on $X$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Computation of the spin connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement:
The spin connection is then computed by decomposing the structure equation as
$$\begin{cases}d\theta^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge \theta^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge \theta^4=0
\cr
d\theta^4+\omega^4{}_i\wedge \theta^i=0, \end{cases}$$
or, equivalently 
$$\begin{cases}
de^i-\frac{1}{\rho}d\rho\wedge e^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge e^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge d\rho=0
\cr
\omega^4{}_i\wedge e^i=0.\end{cases}$$
These equations can be readily solved in terms of the (co-)triad $e^i$ and the associated $\gamma$-compatible spin connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j$
$$\begin{cases}
\omega^i{}_j={}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)-\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)d\rho
\cr
\omega^{4i}=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j.
\end{cases}$$
Here dot denotes the derivative with respect to $\rho$, and $\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)$ is the metric product of 1-forms $\dot e^i$ and $e^j$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: decompose the torsion-free structure equations in the adapted coframe and solve for $\omega$.

nodes.name: Self-dual Levi-Civita connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement:
We may now express the $SU(2)$-connection $A^i$ in terms of the 1-parameter families of (co-)frames and spin connections on $X$ as
\begin{eqnarray} A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+{}^\gamma\omega^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}\gamma(\dot e^j,e^k)d\rho,
\end{eqnarray}
where ${}^\gamma\omega^i=-(1/2)\epsilon^{ijk}\, {}^\gamma\omega^{jk}$.

nodes.statement_short: The self-dual SU(2) connection of an AH metric has a $1/\rho$ pole $e^i/\rho$ plus the boundary spin connection and $\dot e$ terms.

nodes.name: General form of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement:
Thus, in general, an asymptotically hyperbolic ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection may be written as:
\begin{eqnarray} A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i_{(0)}+\omega^i_{(0)}+a^i+b^id\rho
\end{eqnarray}
where
\[ a^i=a^i_{(0)}+\rho a^i_{(1)}+\cdots, \qquad b^i=b^i_{(0)}+\rho b^i_{(1)}+\cdots \]
are 1-parameter families of 1-forms and functions on $X$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: An AH connection is $e_{(0)}/\rho+\omega_{(0)}+a+b\,d\rho$ with $a,b$ power series in $\rho$.
conclusions: A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i_{(0)}+\omega^i_{(0)}+a^i+b^id\rho

This should be contrasted to the metric case, where the requirement (\ref{FG}) of a second-order pole only gives the conformal compactness condition and an extra condition must be imposed to obtain asymptotically hyperbolic metrics.

nodes.statement_short: A first-order pole of the connection already forces asymptotic field equations, whereas a metric pole gives only conformal compactness.

nodes.name: Evolution and constraint equations
nodes.statement: The first set of equations can be viewed as evolution equations for the momentum 2-forms $\pi^i$. However, it is better to think of them as first-order evolution equations for the matrix $M^{ij}$. The matrix $M^{ij}$ then determines $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), which in turn determines the evolution of $\alpha^i$ via (\ref{X-alpha}). The second set of equations are the constraints that the matrix $M^{ij}$ should satisfy, relating $M^{ij}$ to $X^{ij}$. One of the important features of the connection formulation is that there are only 3 constraint equations to be satisfied, to be compared with 4 diffeomorphism constraints in the metric approach.
nodes.statement_short: The first equations evolve $M$ (then $X$, then $\alpha$); the second are only 3 constraints versus 4 in the metric approach.

$$\alpha^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$
with
$$ e^i = e^i_{(0)} + \rho \, e^i_{(1)} + \ldots,$$
and $\omega_{(0)}$ being the Levi-Civita connection of the frame $e_{(0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha^i=e^i/\rho+\omega_{(0)}^i$ with $e^i$ a power series in $\rho$ starting at the boundary frame $e_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: Temporal gauge differs from the Fefferman--Graham gauge
nodes.statement: Note that the gauge-fixing condition $\beta^i=0$ is not compatible with the gauge used in the metric setting, see (\ref{FG}). Indeed, as we have previously computed, the connection corresponding to metric (\ref{FG}) is of the form (\ref{A-metric}), and in particular has a $d\rho$ term. The gauge $\beta^i=0$, quite convenient in calculations, will thus fail to produce a metric in the gauge (\ref{FG}). This just means that the most natural coordinate systems used in the metric and connection settings are different.

conclusions: all the divergent terms in (\ref{action}) are the same as those in the functional

nodes.name: Divergences as Chern--Simons functional
nodes.statement: \frac{3}{\Lambda}\int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon}[A] ,
nodes.label: bulk-bound

nodes.name: Direct computation of the divergences
nodes.statement:
\int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = -2 \int_{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} (3 + \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(f)) + \ldots=
-\frac{2}{\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 - \frac{2}{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 \,{\rm Tr}(f)+ \ldots,

nodes.name: Renormalised volume (connection setting)
nodes.statement:
We define it as
\begin{eqnarray} -2 \Lambda \, RV= \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left( \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) + \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon} \right),
\end{eqnarray}
where we took (\ref{volume}) into account.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume via Chern--Simons
nodes.statement: -2 \Lambda \, RV= \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left( \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) + \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon} \right),
nodes.label: RV-CS

nodes.name: Different $1/\epsilon$ coefficient from the metric setup
nodes.statement: We note that the coefficient in front of $1/\epsilon$ term in our connection setup is different from that in the metric setup, see (\ref{RV}). This is because we are working in a different gauge and the metric as computed from the connection would have had the mixed $d\rho dx^i$ terms. These would change the computation of the renormalised volume above. There would be extra sub-leading terms present that would change the coefficient in front of the $1/\epsilon$ term.

nodes.name: Large gauge transformations of the Chern--Simons functional
nodes.statement: However, as is well-known, Chern--Simons functional is not gauge invariant. It remains invariant under small gauge transformations (homotopic to the identity). Under the so-called large gauge transformations, Chern--Simons functional changes (in our normalisation) by an integral multiple of $8\pi^2$, so that $S^{CS}/4\pi$ changes by a multiple of $2\pi$. More precisely, there is a natural isomorphism $H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$; now given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle, write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong {\mathbb Z}$, then $S^{CS}(g^*(A)) = 8\pi^2 n + S^{CS}(A)$.
nodes.statement_short: Chern--Simons is invariant under small gauge transformations but shifts by $8\pi^2 n$, $n$ the degree, under large ones.
assumptions: given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle, write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong {\mathbb Z}$

nodes.name: Renormalised volume defined modulo a constant
conclusions: RV\in \mathbb{R}\quad {\rm mod} \quad \frac{3}{2\Lambda^2} 8\pi^2.

nodes.name: Ambiguity of renormalised volume
nodes.statement: RV\in \mathbb{R}\quad {\rm mod} \quad \frac{3}{2\Lambda^2} 8\pi^2.

nodes.name: On-shell Einstein--Hilbert action is a multiple of the volume
conclusions: S = -\frac{\Lambda}{8\pi G} V.

nodes.name: Einstein--Hilbert action
nodes.statement: S_{\rm EH} = -\frac{1}{16\pi G} \int \sqrt{g} (R-2\Lambda)

nodes.name: On-shell Einstein--Hilbert action
nodes.statement: S = -\frac{\Lambda}{8\pi G} V.
nodes.label: S-EH-on-shell

nodes.name: Path integral over connections
nodes.statement: \int {\cal D}A \, \exp{\frac{i}{\hbar} S[A]}.

nodes.name: Argument for the ambiguity of the connection action
nodes.statement: As we have described above, our action in the connection setting is just a multiple of the total volume of the space, and we should clearly use the same multiple as in (\ref{S-EH-on-shell}). Now, as we discussed, in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting we need to add a multiple of the Chern--Simons functional of the boundary connection to our bulk action, to regularise it and to make the variational principle well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: the action is a multiple of the volume plus a Chern--Simons boundary term, which is defined only modulo $8\pi^2$.

nodes.name: Connection action defined modulo a constant
conclusions: S  \in \mathbb{R} \quad {\rm (mod)} \quad \frac{3}{8 G \Lambda} 2\pi.

nodes.name: Ambiguity of the action
nodes.statement: S  \in \mathbb{R} \quad {\rm (mod)} \quad \frac{3}{8 G \Lambda} 2\pi.

nodes.name: Quantisation of the cosmological constant
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness of $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ forces $1/(8G\hbar)=N\Lambda/3$, i.e. $L^2=8Nl_P^2$.
assumptions: If we want the path integral to be insensitive to this ambiguity
conclusions: \frac{1}{8 G \hbar} = \frac{N\Lambda}{3}, \qquad N\in {\mathbb N}.

nodes.name: Quantisation condition
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{8 G \hbar} = \frac{N\Lambda}{3}, \qquad N\in {\mathbb N}.

nodes.name: Extrapolation to positive cosmological constant
nodes.statement: Of course, we have derived the above quantisation condition working with asymptotically hyperbolic connections corresponding to negative scalar curvature. Observations indicate that our Universe is filled with dark energy whose equation of state is consistent with having a {\it positive} cosmological constant. If we extrapolate (\ref{quant}) to the setting of positive $\Lambda$, then, for all quantities as observed $N$ is very large $8N = L^2/l_P^2 \sim 10^{120}$, and is the number embodying the famous cosmological constant problem.

nodes.name: Analogy with three-dimensional gravity
nodes.statement: It should also be said that the quantisation condition (\ref{quant}) is reminiscent of what happens in the setting of Riemannian signature gravity in three dimensions (with positive $\Lambda$), where the full action, not just the boundary term as here, is given by the Chern-Simons functional of a certain ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection. Similar large gauge transformation considerations show that the cosmological constant must be quantised in this setting, see e.g., \cite{Freidel:1998ua} where this fact is reviewed.

nodes.name: Analogy with Anderson's Chern--Gauss--Bonnet renormalisation
nodes.statement: We also note that the fact that the Chern--Simons functional renormalises the volume is analogous to the statement in \cite{Anderson} that the boundary term at infinity in the Chern--Gauss--Bonnet formula renormalises the volume. The statement in this paper is similar, except that we use the integral of the first Pontryagin density of the bundle, not the Euler density, for the renormalisation.

nodes.name: Partial gauge fixing by infinitesimal diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations
nodes.statement:
Under an infinitesimal diffeomorphism generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and infinitesimal gauge transformation generated by $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\mathfrak {su}(2))$ the connection (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) transformations as
\begin{multline*}
\delta_{\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho+\varphi}A^i





=\frac{1}{\rho}({\mathcal L}^X_\xi e^i_{(0)}+\epsilon^{ijk}e^j_{(0)}\varphi^k-\lambda e^i_{(0)})
\\
+{\mathcal L}^X_\xi \omega^i_{(0)}+d^X\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\omega_{(0)}^j\varphi^k+{\mathcal L}^X_\xi a^i+\epsilon^{ijk}a^j\varphi^k+\rho(\lambda \dot a^i+b^id^X\lambda)
\\
+\Big(\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)\Big)d\rho
\end{multline*}
The idea now is to set $b^i$ and the anti-symmetric and trace parts of (the subleading orders of) $\langle a^i,e^j_{(0)}\rangle$ to zero by (infinitesimal) diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations. Indeed, we may impose
$$b^i+\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)=0,$$
\begin{multline*}
\epsilon^{ijk}\langle a^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{2}{\rho}\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle d^X\varphi^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle
\\
+\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle \varphi^i-\langle \omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle \varphi^k+\langle a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^i-\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k
\\
+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}_\xi^Xa^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi}e^j_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle
+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi}\omega_{(0)}^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle
\\
+\rho(\lambda\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \dot a^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\epsilon^{ijk}b^j\langle d^X\lambda,e^k_{(0)}\rangle)=0,
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
\langle a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\frac{3}{\rho}\lambda+\rho(\lambda\langle \dot a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+b^k\langle d^X\lambda,e^k_{(0)}\rangle)
\\
+\langle{\mathcal L}_\xi^Xa^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi}e^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi}\omega_{(0)}^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle
\\
+\langle d^X\varphi^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\epsilon^{klm}\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^l_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^m-\epsilon^{klm}\langle a^k,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^m=0,
\end{multline*}
which can be solved recursively starting with, say, $\xi_{(0)}=0$, $\varphi_{(0)}^i=0$ and $\lambda_{(0)}=0$.
nodes.section: A Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
nodes.statement_short: Compute the infinitesimal gauge+diffeomorphism variation of the connection and solve recursively for generators killing $b$ and the antisymmetric/trace parts.

nodes.name: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
nodes.statement:
We can thus partially gauge fix the diffeomorphism and gauge freedom restricting our considerations to asymptotically hyperbolic connections of the form
$$A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$
with $e^i$ symmetric and trace 3 with respect to the frame $e^i_{(0)}$.
nodes.section: A Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
conclusions: $$A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$ with $e^i$ symmetric and trace 3 with respect to the frame $e^i_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: Residual gauge freedom
nodes.statement:
There still remains some diffeomorphism and gauge freedom: infinitesimal diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\mathfrak {su}(2))$ satisfying
$$\frac{1}{\rho}\dot \xi^i+\dot \xi^k\langle\omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\dot\varphi^i+\dot \xi^k\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle=0,$$
\begin{multline*}
\frac{2}{\rho}(\varphi^i-\varphi_{(0)}^i)+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle d^X(\varphi^j-\varphi_{(0)}^j),e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^i-\varphi_{(0)}^i)-\langle \omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^k-\varphi_{(0)}^k)
\\
+\langle a^k,e^i_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k_{(0)}-\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k+2\langle d^X\lambda_{(0)},e^i_{(0)}\rangle
\\
+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}_\xi^Xa^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}e^j_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle
+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}\omega_{(0)}^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle
-\epsilon^{ijk}\langle a^j,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi_{(0)}} e^l_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle=0,
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
-\frac{3}{\rho}(\lambda-\lambda_{(0)})
+\langle{\mathcal L}_\xi^Xa^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}e^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}\omega_{(0)}^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle
-\langle a^k,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\langle {\mathcal L}^X_{\xi_{(0)}} e^l_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle 
\\
+\langle d^X(\varphi^k-\varphi_{(0)}^k),e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\epsilon^{klm}\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^l_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^m-\varphi_{(0)}^m)=0,
\end{multline*}
for arbitrary $\xi_{(0)}\in\Gamma(TX)$,$\lambda_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X)$ and $\varphi^i_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X,\mathfrak {su}(2))$, do not alter the form of the connection. These equations can again be solved recursively leading to a residual boundary diffeomorphism, rescaling and gauge freedom.
nodes.section: A Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
nodes.statement_short: Generators satisfying recursive equations with arbitrary boundary data preserve the gauge, leaving boundary diffeomorphisms, rescalings and gauge freedom.
conclusions: These equations can again be solved recursively leading to a residual boundary diffeomorphism, rescaling and gauge freedom.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian derivation of the 3+1 field equations
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Dirac constraint analysis: Legendre transform the 3+1 Lagrangian, impose primary and secondary constraints, and read off Hamilton's equations.

nodes.name: 3+1 Lagrangian
nodes.statement: S[A,M,\mu] = \int_M \left( M^{ij} f_\alpha^{i} \wedge \left(  \dot\alpha^{j}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j}\right) - \mu \, g(M) \right) \wedge d\rho.
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Generalised Hamiltonian
nodes.statement:
H[\alpha, \pi, \beta, \pi_{\beta}, M , \pi_M ,u,v,w] = \int_X -\beta^{i}\left( d^X_\alpha\pi^i \right)  + \mu \, g(M) \\ 
+ u^i \wedge  \left(\pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha\right) + v^i \wedge \pi^i_{\beta} + w^{ij} \wedge \pi^{ij}_M + x \pi_{\mu}
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Second secondary constraint
nodes.statement: \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} = X^{ij}
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.label: apdx: sec ctr

nodes.name: Remaining constraint analysis
nodes.statement: In principle, we should also take care of the secondary constraint $\left\{ H , \pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha \right\}=0$ together with tertiary constraints possibly arising. We do not carry out this analysis here as it is not necessary to obtain the field equations. We also note that one way to complete the Hamiltonian analysis is via an Ashtekar-like Hamiltonian formulation, which for modified theories considered here was described in \cite{Krasnov:2008zz}.
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Decompose the structure equations
nodes.statement:
The spin connection is then computed by decomposing the structure equation as
$$\begin{cases}d\theta^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge \theta^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge \theta^4=0
\cr
d\theta^4+\omega^4{}_i\wedge \theta^i=0, \end{cases}$$
or, equivalently 
$$\begin{cases}
de^i-\frac{1}{\rho}d\rho\wedge e^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge e^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge d\rho=0
\cr
\omega^4{}_i\wedge e^i=0.\end{cases}$$
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: Write the torsion-free structure equations in the adapted coframe.

nodes.name: Solve for the spin connection
nodes.statement:
These equations can be readily solved in terms of the (co-)triad $e^i$ and the associated $\gamma$-compatible spin connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j$
$$\begin{cases}
\omega^i{}_j={}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)-\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)d\rho
\cr
\omega^{4i}=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j.
\end{cases}$$
Here dot denotes the derivative with respect to $\rho$, and $\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)$ is the metric product of 1-forms $\dot e^i$ and $e^j$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: Solve the structure equations for $\omega^i{}_j$ and $\omega^{4i}$.

nodes.name: Wedge matrix is asymptotically identity
nodes.statement: As is clear from (\ref{curv-asympt}), asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: From the curvature asymptotics, $X\sim\delta$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary matrix is asymptotically pure trace
nodes.statement: From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $X(M)$ relation to get $M\sim\delta$.

nodes.name: Field equation reduces to Bianchi identity
nodes.statement: This in particular implies that the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) is automatically satisfied, as it reduces to the Bianchi identity for the curvature.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: With $M\propto\mathbb I$ the connection equation is the Bianchi identity.

nodes.name: Combine the two expansions
nodes.statement: We now combine (\ref{X-soln}) and (\ref{M-soln}) to compute the divergent contributions.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the wedge-product matrix with the $M$ expansion.

nodes.name: Leading term is pure trace
nodes.statement: The leading term in (\ref{X-soln}) is a multiple of the identity matrix.
nodes.statement_short: The leading wedge matrix is proportional to the identity.

nodes.name: Trace-free part drops out
nodes.statement: Hence, because of the trace free character of the order $\rho^3$ term in (\ref{M-soln}), there is no contribution from that term and this is why it was not necessary to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: The trace-free $\rho^3$ term of $M$ gives no divergent contribution.

nodes.name: Goal of the appendix
nodes.statement: We here show how to derive the 3+1 decomposition of the field equations described in \ref{subsec: Init val form} from a Hamiltonian formulation.
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Aim: rederive the 3+1 equations from a Hamiltonian formulation.

nodes.name: 3+1 decomposition of the connection and curvature
nodes.statement:
As before, we decompose the connection $A^i$ as  
$$A^i=\alpha^i+\beta^id\rho,$$
and its curvature as
$$F_A^i=f_\alpha^i-(\dot\alpha^i-d^X_\alpha\beta^i)\wedge d\rho,$$
where $d^X_\alpha$ is the covariant exterior derivative with respect to connection $\alpha^i$ along the hypersurface $\rho=\text{const}$, and $f^i_\alpha$ is the curvature of $\alpha^i$. The matrix $X^{ij}$, defined up to scale, now reads
\[
X^{ij} {\mathcal V}= F^i \wedge F^j =  f_\alpha^{(i}\wedge (\dot\alpha^{j)}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j)})\wedge d\rho.
 \]
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Recall the 3+1 split of $A$, its curvature and the wedge matrix $X$.

nodes.name: 3+1 Lagrangian
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the action in 3+1 form with a 3-form multiplier $\mu$.

nodes.name: Primary constraints from the momenta
nodes.statement:
The associated momenta are:
\begin{align*}
\pi^i := \pi^i_{\alpha} = M^{ij} f^i_\alpha \;; & &
\pi^i_{\beta}=0 \;; & &
\pi^{ij}_M =0 \;; & & \pi_{\mu}=0.
\end{align*}
Note that $\dot{\alpha}$ do not appear in the right-hand-side of the first equation, thus we cannot invert the system and write $\pi_{\alpha}$ as a function of $\dot{\alpha}$. The same is true for all other momenta. This means that we have to keep track of the above equations as constraints on the phase space.
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: The momenta cannot be inverted for velocities, giving primary constraints.

nodes.name: Generalised Hamiltonian
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Form the total Hamiltonian with Lagrange multipliers for all primary constraints.

nodes.name: Secondary constraints
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Preservation of primary constraints yields the Gauss constraint, the $M$-equation and $g(M)=0$.

nodes.name: Hamilton's equations
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Write Hamilton's equations for $\pi$ and $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Recover the field equations
nodes.section: B Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate $u$ to recover (29) and the $M$-equation (75).
